title: Principles of Information Security
subtitle: Climb the money ladder — one question per grade level

questions.q: Which component of the CIA Triad ensures that data is only accessible to authorized users?
questions.note: Confidentiality prevents unauthorized disclosure of information. Controls include encryption, access control lists, and need-to-know policies.

explain.correct: Confidentiality is the CIA pillar ensuring data is disclosed only to authorized users -- enforced via encryption, access controls, and least privilege.
wrong: Availability is about data being reachable when needed, not who may see it.
Integrity is about data not being altered without authorization, not access restriction.
Non-repudiation proves an action cannot be denied and isn't one of the three CIA pillars.

questions.q: Which type of threat actor is most likely motivated by financial gain and typically operates as part of an organized criminal syndicate?
questions.note: Cybercriminals are motivated primarily by financial gain. They often work in organized groups and conduct ransomware attacks, fraud, and data theft.

explain.correct: Cybercriminals are profit-driven and often operate in organized syndicates running ransomware, fraud, and data theft.
wrong: Hacktivists act on ideology or a political cause, not money.
Nation-state actors pursue espionage or strategic goals for a government, not personal profit.
Script kiddies use others' tools for thrills and lack a syndicate's organization.

questions.q: An attacker calls a hospital's IT help desk, impersonates a physician, and convinces a technician to reset a password without verification. This is an example of:
questions.note: Pretexting is fabricating a scenario (pretext) to manipulate a victim into providing access or information. Impersonating a physician to reset credentials is a classic pretexting attack.

explain.correct: Pretexting builds a fabricated scenario -- here, posing as a physician -- to manipulate the target into acting.
wrong: Phishing uses fraudulent messages (usually email) to many people; this was a targeted call with a crafted backstory.
Vishing is voice phishing; the defining element here is the invented persona and scenario, i.e. pretexting.
Tailgating is following someone through a physical door, not a phone con.

questions.q: Which symmetric encryption algorithm uses a 128, 192, or 256-bit key and is the current US federal standard?
questions.note: AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) was adopted by NIST in 2001 as the federal standard. It supports 128, 192, and 256-bit key sizes and is used in TLS, disk encryption, and Wi-Fi security.

explain.correct: AES is the symmetric block cipher (128/192/256-bit keys) adopted as the US federal standard in FIPS 197.
wrong: DES uses a 56-bit key and is obsolete and insecure.
3DES applies DES three times; deprecated by NIST and far slower than AES.
RC4 is a broken stream cipher, not the 128/192/256-bit block standard.

questions.q: A stateful firewall differs from a stateless packet filter because it:
options: Tracks the state of active connections and allows only packets belonging to established sessions
Blocks all inbound traffic by default
Inspects application-layer content for malware signatures
Operates at Layer 7 of the OSI model
questions.note: A stateful firewall maintains a connection state table and only allows packets that are part of an established, legitimate session. Stateless filters inspect each packet in isolation.

explain.correct: A stateful firewall tracks active connections and permits only packets that belong to an established session.
wrong: Default-deny on inbound is a policy any firewall can apply -- not what makes it stateful.
Inspecting application-layer content for malware is deep packet inspection / NGFW behavior.
Operating at Layer 7 describes an application or proxy firewall; stateful inspection works at Layers 3-4.

questions.q: Which network security zone is designed to host public-facing services while isolating them from the internal network?
questions.note: A DMZ sits between the internet and the internal network, typically protected by two firewalls. Public services run here, limiting the blast radius if they are compromised.

explain.correct: A DMZ is a perimeter zone that hosts public-facing services while isolating them from the internal network.
wrong: A VLAN segments a LAN logically but isn't specifically the public-facing isolation zone.
An intranet is the internal private network -- what a DMZ protects, not the exposed zone.
An air-gapped network has no external connectivity at all, the opposite of hosting public services.

questions.q: Multi-factor authentication (MFA) requires users to present factors from at least two of three categories. Which answer correctly lists all three categories?
options: Something you know, something you have, something you are
Something you know, something you have, something you feel
questions.note: The three authentication factors are: something you know (password/PIN), something you have (token/smart card), and something you are (biometric). MFA requires at least two different categories.

explain.correct: The three authentication factor categories are something you know, something you have, and something you are (a biometric).
wrong: 'Something you feel' is not a recognized authentication factor category.
Username, password, and PIN are all 'something you know' -- one category, not three.
Smart card and biometric are valid factors, but an IP address is not a factor category.

questions.q: Which access control model grants or denies access based on sensitivity labels assigned to subjects and objects?
questions.note: MAC uses classification labels (e.g., Top Secret, Secret, Unclassified). Access is determined by policy, not the data owner. It is common in government and military environments.

explain.correct: Mandatory Access Control grants access by system-assigned sensitivity labels and clearances; the owner cannot override it.
wrong: RBAC grants access by job role, not sensitivity labels.
DAC lets the resource owner decide access, not a system-enforced label scheme.
ABAC uses attributes and policies rather than classification labels specifically.

questions.q: According to NIST SP 800-61, what is the correct order of incident response phases?
options: Detection, Containment, Eradication, Recovery, Lessons Learned
Preparation, Detection and Analysis, Containment, Eradication and Recovery, Post-Incident Activity
questions.note: NIST SP 800-61 defines four IR phases: Preparation; Detection and Analysis; Containment, Eradication, and Recovery; Post-Incident Activity (lessons learned). This is the authoritative framework.

explain.correct: NIST SP 800-61's lifecycle is Preparation; Detection and Analysis; Containment, Eradication and Recovery; and Post-Incident Activity.
wrong: This omits the critical first phase, Preparation, and mis-splits the later phases.
'Identification' and 'Reporting' are not the NIST 800-61 phase names.
Triage/Isolation/Remediation/Reporting/Closure is an ad-hoc flow, not the NIST 800-61 lifecycle.

questions.q: Which hashing algorithm produces a 256-bit digest and is widely used in TLS certificates and code signing?
questions.note: SHA-256 (part of the SHA-2 family) produces a 256-bit hash and is the current standard for TLS certificates and code signing. MD5 and SHA-1 are considered cryptographically broken.

explain.correct: SHA-256 produces a 256-bit digest and is widely used in TLS certificates and code signing.
wrong: MD5 produces a 128-bit digest and is cryptographically broken.
SHA-1 produces a 160-bit digest and is deprecated due to collision attacks.
RIPEMD-128 produces a 128-bit digest and is rarely used in modern TLS.

questions.q: A data classification policy assigns the label "Restricted" to personally identifiable information (PII). Which US governance framework mandates protection of this data in healthcare?
questions.note: HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act) mandates the protection of Protected Health Information (PHI). It requires appropriate safeguards including data classification and access controls.

explain.correct: HIPAA is the US law mandating protection of health information (PHI); classifying PII as 'Restricted' in a healthcare setting enforces it.
wrong: SOC 2 is a voluntary auditing standard for service-provider controls, not a healthcare legal mandate.
PCI-DSS governs payment-card data, not health records.
ISO 27001 is an international infosec management standard, not a US healthcare mandate.
